checkpoints: A media query answers "how wide is the screen", but a component actually cares about "how wide is my slot" — that gap is exactly what container queries fill.
Because `@media` cannot distinguish between different slots at the same viewport, the layout decision is forced out to be hand-enumerated at the page level instead of owned by the component itself.

That hand-enumeration takes the form of a `variant` prop every call site must remember to pass correctly — multiplied across every slot × breakpoint combination, this is what "media-query soup" means as the system grows.

Declaring `container-type: inline-size` on a wrapper turns that wrapper into a query container, establishing containment on the inline axis so every `@container` query inside now measures the wrapper's own width instead of the viewport's.

The key constraint is that the container must be an ancestor of the element placing the query, since an element cannot measure itself — which is why a wrapper layer around the component is always required.

As a result the component contains all of its own responsive logic and is correct in any slot with no control prop at all — an inversion of control that eliminates the need to enumerate the slot × breakpoint combination at the page level.

Observable proof: the same `ProductCard`, at one exact viewport, renders compact in a 260px sidebar and rich in a 720px main column simultaneously, purely because the two containers differ in width while the viewport never changed.
The browser cannot know an image's height until the file header bytes arrive over the network, so an `` with no `width`/`height`/`aspect-ratio` is forced to render at height 0.
When the image finishes loading and the browser learns the real height, it inserts that height and pushes everything below it down — that single event is a layout shift.
CLS is the sum of every such shift on the page, excluding shifts caused by recent user input, which is why many small pops — not just one big jump — can fail the metric.

Dimension reservation fixes this by giving the browser `width`/`height` or a CSS `aspect-ratio` so it can compute the box height from the known width before any bytes arrive, reserving the slot so the image never has to move.
This only works if the declared ratio is actually correct, since a wrong ratio distorts or crops the image.
With a `srcset` serving several resolutions, every variant must share that one aspect ratio, though `object-fit: cover` can absorb small mismatches without reflowing.

Verify the fix by installing a `PerformanceObserver` on `layout-shift` entries and summing their `value` (ignoring `hadRecentInput`) — the total should stay near zero after every image on the page has settled.
This PR should not merge as-is — it only "looks fine" because the JPEG fallback path happens to still be correct, which is exactly what hides two other dead branches.
`<picture>` is evaluated top-down: the browser commits to the first `<source>` that matches both `media` and a supported `type`, and never looks further.

Defect one: the wide-format sources are ordered JPEG, WebP, AVIF, but since every browser supports JPEG the browser always commits to it first, so the WebP/AVIF sources beneath it are unreachable dead code.

Defect two: the mobile art-direction source sits below the unconditioned wide sources, so on a narrow viewport the browser still matches the unconditioned JPEG first and the square crop can never be reached — media-conditioned sources must precede unconditioned ones because framing is decided before format.

The fix reorders both problems as one rule: media-conditioned sources first (most-modern format inside), then unconditioned format sources most-modern-first (AVIF, WebP), with the `` JPEG last as the universal fallback carrying `alt`/`width`/`height`.

Defect three: the gallery thumbnail's `srcSet` uses `1x`/`2x` descriptors on an image styled `width: 100%` inside a fluid grid track, but `x` descriptors switch purely by device-pixel-ratio and ignore the image's real CSS width; fix by replacing them with `w` descriptors plus a `sizes` value that mirrors the grid column's real width.

Proof of the fix: assert `currentSrc` contains `.avif` on an AVIF-capable browser at desktop width, contains the square-crop URL below 640px, and — for the thumb — resolves to a different candidate at a narrow vs. a wide viewport, checked with a strict inequality rather than only membership in the candidate set.

By default, every image on the page — the hero included — is queued at Low priority until the browser finishes layout and learns what's actually in the viewport; since the hero and the 12 thumbnails are all eager at that same default, they compete for identical bandwidth with nothing telling the browser the hero matters more, which is why it finishes last despite being first in the DOM.
An image's URL is discovered only once the HTML parser reaches that image's own `` tag, which is a separate problem from priority ranking.
Fix: add a `` for the hero's exact URL in `` so the preload scanner finds it at head-parse time regardless of where the `` sits in the body.
Fix: mark only the hero `` with `fetchpriority="high"` so it is explicitly ranked above every other image once discovered.
Fix: add `loading="lazy"` to the thumbnails so they stop contending for bandwidth during the initial load, leaving anything already in the initial viewport besides the hero untouched at default.

Anti-pattern to avoid: blanket-raising `fetchpriority="high"` on the thumbnails too — bandwidth is finite, so raising everyone's priority evenly is mathematically the same as raising no one's, and can crowd out render-blocking CSS/JS that deserves priority ahead of any image.

Prove the fix via network inspection: the hero's request should show `initialPriority: "High"` and start right after head-parse, and a `largest-contentful-paint` `PerformanceObserver` entry should confirm the hero is still the LCP element with a measurably lower timestamp.

Watch for one regression: if the preloaded URL in `` doesn't exactly match the `src` the component actually renders (different query param, different CDN transform), the browser fetches the image twice — once for the preload, once for the real `` — wasting bandwidth instead of saving time.

Static import of HeavyWidget merges its chunk into the main bundle, so every visitor downloads and parses it before first render even though the component only renders conditionally on showWidget, including 3G visitors who never scroll far enough to trigger it.

Fix: switch to lazy(() => import("./HeavyWidget")) and render it only when !constrained AND the anchor is near the viewport via IntersectionObserver, so constrained visitors never trigger a chunk request and see a lightweight deferred placeholder instead.
The prefetch useEffect fires unconditionally on mount, competing for bandwidth with the content the visitor is waiting on and burning exactly the data saveData was meant to save.
Fix: gate the prefetch behind effectiveType === "4g" AND !constrained AND deviceMemory >= 4, treating it as spending spare capacity rather than a default.
autoPlay is hard-wired on the hero video regardless of any data-saving signal; fix: drop autoPlay whenever saveData/reducedData is on.
Keep the constrained/capable signal coarse rather than fragmenting it into finer network/RAM tiers.

Verify by injecting constrained (3g/saveData) and capable (4g/high-deviceMemory) profiles and asserting the widget chunk/prefetch link only appear for the capable case while the deferred placeholder renders for the constrained case.
Verify separately via a bundle-analysis pass confirming HeavyWidget genuinely split out of the main chunk, not just "looks right" in the source.
The Card's public API accepts only data/content props; no layout-control prop is allowed to cross the boundary.
The Card renders its own internal wrapper declaring container-type: inline-size, since an element can't query its own width and letting the consumer declare containment would leak the contract.
Compact vs rich layout switches via internal container breakpoints (around ~320px container width) that the component itself owns and documents, invisible to the caller.
Typography scales with clamp(min, a cqi-based value, max) so type tracks the slot's width rather than the viewport, preserving true slot independence.

The consumer controls exactly one variable — the slot's width; a variant="compact" escape hatch is rejected because it pulls the layout decision back to every call-site, recreating the media-query-soup failure mode container queries exist to kill, so the only sanctioned lever is narrowing the slot itself.

The contract guarantees overflow-safety at any width via intrinsic sizing and min-width: 0 on inner content, making the Card drop-in-correct in a sidebar, main column, modal, or dashboard tile with zero extra configuration.

width, height, and alt are mandatory props (not optional, no default) because they let the browser compute the box's aspect-ratio/height before any image byte arrives, reserving the slot and guaranteeing CLS = 0; making them optional would allow shipping a dimensionless image, while making them mandatory turns a missing dimension into a compile-time TypeScript error — CLS-by-construction rather than by developer discipline.

The component stays passive about WHEN to load: src is typed string | undefined and the component only renders what it's given; the timing decision belongs to the caller, implemented via a lazy hook (e.g. useLazyImage using IntersectionObserver + rootMargin) that swaps in the real src once the element enters the observation band.

The hero/LCP image must never be deferred; baking laziness into the component would force an escape-hatch flag like bypassLazy for that exact case — a sign the decision belongs outside the component — whereas keeping it passive lets the hero simply pass its real src from the start with no flag at all.

A single component serves both extremes because of that passive boundary: thumbnails gate src via lazy visibility while the hero always passes its real src plus fetchPriority="high" (other images default to "auto"); fetchPriority is caller-declared intent the component merely forwards to the DOM attribute, since only the page knows which element is its LCP.

An lqip prop carries a small base64 data URI rendered as a blurred placeholder beneath the sharp image with zero extra network request; when the sharp image's load event fires, the component flips to a loaded state and runs an opacity crossfade — guaranteed once inside the component rather than reimplemented at every call-site.

Against a simpler "just src + alt" API: that leaves CLS as a forgettable convention, whereas the mandatory-dimensions contract makes a dimensionless image impossible to ship; the only remaining caller responsibility is marking exactly one image as hero/high-priority (marking several defeats prioritization) and never lazy-gating it, at the cost of every call-site needing to plumb real width/height/lqip data through to the props.

Candidate selection is based on sizes × viewport × DPR, and the browser must finish computing it before layout runs because the preload scanner wants to start downloading the image very early, without waiting to measure the real display width after layout.
sizes is the developer's pre-layout promise about the image's display width.

With no sizes declared, the browser defaults to treating the image as 100vw wide, so on a wide desktop viewport it picks the largest srcset candidate — exactly why every 400px card still downloads the 1200w file.

DPR multiplies the device pixels needed (a 400px slot at DPR 2 needs roughly 800 device pixels), so a correctly declared sizes pulls down the 800w candidate — why retina phones look sharp yet still end up heavy on data if sizes over-assumes.
Fix: declare sizes matching the real CSS width at each breakpoint (e.g. (max-width: 640px) 100vw, 400px).
Verify with img.currentSrc — the property reflecting the candidate the browser actually chose — across each emulated viewport/DPR.

Read real runtime capability signals instead of guessing from the user-agent: navigator.connection.effectiveType and saveData (Network Information API), prefers-reduced-data via matchMedia, and navigator.deviceMemory for RAM tier — each behind feature-detection so missing APIs on Safari/Firefox default to the "capable" branch.

Collapse all signals with a single OR into one constrained boolean: slow network (3g/2g/slow-2g) OR saveData OR prefers-reduced-data, since the two data-saver signals are independent (a user can enable prefers-reduced-data at the OS level without the browser ever setting saveData) so either alone must trigger the light path.
A constrained user's payload gets the low image variant with no srcset (no path to upgrade), the hero video drops autoplay, and the heavy widget stays deferred so its JS chunk is never fetched.
A capable user's payload gets a full srcset/sizes so the browser picks by DPR and layout width, plus the normal experience.

Branch only coarsely into two groups rather than many fine tiers, because effectiveType is a fluctuating engine estimate and deviceMemory is deliberately rounded coarsely (0.25/0.5/1/2/4/8) to resist fingerprinting, so finer splitting is both less stable and exposes more fingerprinting surface for no real benefit.

These signals are not static: the connection object fires a change event when network type or saveData flips, and prefers-reduced-data is observable via addEventListener too, so the UI must subscribe and re-branch mid-session rather than compute once at page load and leave it stale.

Resolution selection is something the browser can determine entirely on its own: given a developer-declared `sizes` (display width), it combines that with the device DPR to pick the matching candidate from `srcset`.
Framing (crop) is a decision only a developer can make, expressed via `<source media>` — e.g. switching to a different crop below 640px (art direction).
Format preference is also a developer-only decision, expressed via `<source type>` — e.g. preferring AVIF, falling back to WebP, then JPG.
The browser evaluates `<source>` elements top-to-bottom and commits to the first one whose `media` matches and whose `type` is supported, so the written order encodes the priority policy.
`srcset`+`sizes` can still be attached inside a chosen `<source>`, so resolution selection keeps happening there — the two mechanisms stack rather than exclude each other.
The trailing `` is both the universal fallback and the carrier of `alt`/`width`/`height`.
Boundary rule: `srcset`/`sizes` alone is enough when only sharpness must adapt across sizes; `<picture>` becomes necessary once the crop or the format must change.
`w` descriptors (used with `sizes`) suit images that scale with the layout, while `x` descriptors (1x/2x) suit only fixed-size images like logos/avatars, since they ignore the viewport entirely.
